title: Saying exactly what you mean
cando: work out new words from their parts, and describe things precisely

about.text: In this lesson you explain a new product to a colleague who has never seen it, and you learn to say exactly what you mean. You see how prefixes and suffixes build new words, so you can work out words you have never met. Then you read a job specification full of jargon and rewrite it in plain English.
goals: Explain what a product or a tool does, simply and precisely.
Work out new words from their parts: un-, dis-, mis-, -able, -ful and -ness.
Use the right small word after a noun or a verb: a reason for, depend on.
Read a job specification and rewrite it in plain English.
Explain a topic from your work or life to a non-expert, and answer their questions.

chapters.title: Explaining something new
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you explain something new to someone who has never seen it.
Listen to Ana and Samir. They work at a busy car repair garage. The garage has bought a new booking app, and Ana explains it to Samir. Samir is great with engines, but he isn't very technical with computers. So Ana has to be clear.
Listen for three useful phrases. It's a kind of… gives the general idea first, by comparing the new thing with something familiar. It's a kind of online diary.
Basically… gives the main point in a few words. Basically, customers book their own appointments.
What I mean is… says it again, more precisely, when your first try was vague. What I mean is, if you can send a text, you can use it.
A good explanation moves from the general to the precise, and it checks that the listener is following.

chapters.title: Building words
chapters.text:
The grammar in this lesson is about building words.
Many long English words are short words with extra parts. A part at the start is a prefix. Un- and dis- often mean not. Able, unable. Agree, disagree. Mis- means wrongly. Read, misread.
A part at the end is a suffix. -able means you can do it: readable, affordable. -ful means full of something: useful, helpful. -ness turns an adjective into a noun: kind, kindness.
So when you meet a long word you don't know, split it into parts. Unreadable: un, read, able. It cannot be read. Carelessness: care, less, ness. Not taking care.
The second point is the small word that comes after some nouns and verbs. We say a reason for, a solution to, and depend on. It depends on the weather, not of the weather. Learn these pairs as one piece.

chapters.title: In plain English
chapters.text:
In Section 3, you read a job specification. It describes a job, and it lists what the employer wants from applicants.
Like many job specifications, it is full of jargon: words that only people in that line of work understand. Escalate. Triage. First-line resolution.
Your task is to rewrite it in plain English. Use short sentences and everyday words. Keep every fact, but say it so that anyone can follow it.
Here is a good test. Could a friend outside that job read your version once and understand it?

chapters.title: Explaining to a non-expert
chapters.text:
Then it's your turn. Choose a topic you know well: a tool from your job, a process, or a hobby.
Explain it to someone who knows nothing about it. Start with the general idea. Give one clear example. Then say it more precisely.
Your listener will ask questions. Listen carefully to each one. If your first answer was vague, try again: What I mean is…
And check as you go. Does that make sense so far?

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text linked to this lesson.
As you read, stop at one or two long words. Split them into parts, and work out what they mean before you check. You'll be surprised how often it works.

warmup.prompt: A colleague asks you to explain a new app. What do you do first?
choices: tell them what it is for
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people start by saying what it is for, in one sentence. Then they show how it works, one step at a time.

conversation.title: The new booking app
conversation.setting: Ana runs the office at a busy car repair garage. The garage has bought a new booking app, and she explains it to Samir, one of the mechanics.
lines: Samir
Everyone's talking about this new app. What is it, exactly?
Ana
It's a kind of online diary. Basically, customers book their own appointments on their phones.
Samir
OK. But what's the reason for changing? The paper diary works, doesn't it?
Ana
Not always. Half the time the handwriting's unreadable, and people misread the times. Last month we had nine double bookings.
Samir
Nine? I had no idea. So whose fault was that?
Ana
Nobody's, really. It wasn't carelessness. The paper system just isn't reliable.
Samir
And is the app hard to use? I'm good with engines, but I'm not very technical with computers.
Ana
Not at all. It's really user-friendly. What I mean is, if you can send a text, you can use it.
Samir
Will customers need a new phone for it?
Ana
That depends on how old their phone is. It's compatible with almost any smartphone. And it sends a reminder the day before, which is really useful.
Samir
That sounds handy. What happens if the internet goes down?
Ana
Then customers are unable to book online until it's back. In practice, they just phone us instead.
Samir
Fair enough. When does it start?
Ana
We launch it on Monday. I'll demonstrate it to everyone on Friday afternoon.

questions.q: Why does the garage want to stop using the paper diary?
questions.a: The handwriting is hard to read, and there have been double bookings.
wrong: The staff were careless with it.
questions.why: Ana says the handwriting is often unreadable, and they had nine double bookings last month.

questions.q: What does the app do the day before an appointment?
questions.a: It sends the customer a reminder.
questions.why: Ana says: it sends a reminder the day before.

questions.q: What happens in practice if the internet goes down?
wrong: The garage closes for the day.
The app keeps working without it.
questions.why: Ana says: In practice, they just phone us instead.

phrases.text: It's a kind of online diary.
phrases.use: Giving the general idea first, by comparing it with something familiar.

phrases.text: Basically, customers book their own appointments.
phrases.use: Giving the main point in a few words.

phrases.text: What I mean is, if you can send a text, you can use it.
phrases.use: Saying something again more clearly, when the first try was vague.

phrases.text: That depends on how old their phone is.
phrases.use: Saying the answer is different in different situations.

phrases.text: In practice, they just phone us instead.
phrases.use: Saying what really happens, not what should happen in theory.
Offering to show people how something works.

items.meaning: The job that something is designed to do, or one of the jobs it can do.
items.example: The app has one main function: it lets customers book online.

items.meaning: One of the choices on a device or an app that controls how it works, such as the volume or the language.
items.example: You can change the language in the settings menu.

items.meaning: A small, clever piece of equipment, usually electronic, that does one particular job.
items.example: My brother loves gadgets. He's got a speaker that switches the lights on.

items.meaning: Easy for ordinary people to understand and use, without any training.
items.example: The new system is far more user-friendly than the old one.

items.meaning: Able to work together with another device or system without problems.
items.example: Is this charger compatible with my laptop?

items.meaning: Useful and convenient, or easy to reach.
items.example: The reminder text is really handy. I never forget my appointments now.

items.meaning: Working well and quickly, without wasting time, money or energy.
items.example: The new booking system is much more efficient than the paper diary.

items.meaning: Connected with machines, computers or the practical skills of a job. A person described this way understands them well.
items.example: I'm not very technical, so please explain it slowly.

items.meaning: Simple and easy to understand or do, with no hidden problems.
items.example: Setting up the account is straightforward. It takes five minutes.

items.meaning: Exact and accurate, with all the important details.
items.example: Can you give me the precise time of the delivery?

items.meaning: Not clear or detailed enough, so people have to guess what you mean.
items.example: His instructions were so vague that nobody knew what to do.

items.meaning: To start selling or offering a new product or service to the public.
items.example: The company will launch its new app in March.

items.meaning: To change something for a newer and better version.
items.example: We upgraded all the office computers last summer.

items.meaning: To show how something works by using it in front of people.
items.example: The trainer demonstrated the new till before we used it.

items.meaning: In real situations, as opposed to what should happen according to the rules or the plan.
items.example: The rule says lunch is an hour, but in practice most people take thirty minutes.

sound.title: The stress stays on the main word
sound.explain: When you add a part to the start or the end of a word, the strongest beat usually stays where it was, on the main word. Say un-, dis- and mis- lightly, and don't stress -able, -ful or -ness. Listen, then say each group and each line.
lines: Half the time the handwriting's unreadable.
People misread the times.
It's really useful, and it's straightforward to set up.

sayIt.instructions: Say Ana's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Did you say un- and mis- lightly, with the stress on the main word?
lines: It's a kind of online diary. Basically, customers book their own appointments on their phones.
Not always. Half the time the handwriting's unreadable, and people misread the times.
Not at all. It's really user-friendly. What I mean is, if you can send a text, you can use it.
We launch it on Monday. I'll demonstrate it to everyone on Friday afternoon.

spot.instructions: Look at these words and phrases from the conversation. The first five are built from a shorter word, with an extra part at the start or the end. The last two are a noun and a verb that bring their own small word.
examples: That depends on how old their phone is.
spot.question: Find the short word inside each long word. What does each extra part add? And which small word comes after reason, and after depend?
spot.answer: Unreadable is un + read + able: it cannot be read. Misread is mis + read: read wrongly. Carelessness is care + less + ness: the noun for not taking care. Useful is use + ful: full of use. Unable is un + able: not able. We say a reason for something, and it depends on something.

rules.title: Building words: un-, dis-, mis-, -able, -ful, -ness
rule: un- and dis- mean not, or the opposite: unable, unfair, dishonest, disagree, disconnect.
mis- means wrongly: misread, misunderstand, misspell, mislead.
-able means you can do it: readable, affordable, washable. Add un- for the opposite: unreadable.
-ful means full of it: useful, helpful, stressful. Its opposite, -less, means without it: useless, careless.
-ness makes a noun from an adjective: kind, kindness. Aware, awareness. Careless, carelessness.
rules.mistake: Not: unagree or dishappy. Each word takes its own prefix: disagree, unhappy. And -ful has one l: useful, not usefull.

rules.title: A reason for, depend on: the small word that belongs
rule: Some nouns always bring the same small word: a reason for, a solution to, an increase in, an effect on.
Some verbs do too: depend on, apply for, deal with, rely on, listen to.
Learn the pair as one piece: the reason for the delay, not the reason of the delay.
Some verbs take no small word at all: discuss the plan, not discuss about the plan.
After the small word, use -ing for an action: the reason for changing.
rules.mistake: Not: It depends of the weather. Say: It depends on the weather.

practice.q: I can't read this note. The handwriting is ___ .
practice.why: un + read + able: it cannot be read.

practice.q: Sorry, I ___ the email. I thought the meeting was on Tuesday.
practice.why: mis- means wrongly: I read it wrongly.

practice.q: I ___ with the plan. I think it's too expensive.
The reminders are really ___ . Nobody forgets their appointment now.
practice.why: use + ful, with one l: full of use.

practice.q: Thank you for your ___ . You've been very patient with me.
practice.why: -ness makes a noun from the adjective kind.

practice.q: Is there a reason ___ the delay?
practice.why: We say a reason for something.

practice.q: The price depends ___ how many you order.

options: We discussed about the new app.
We discussed on the new app.
practice.why: Discuss takes no small word: you discuss something.

practice.q: The flat is small, but the rent is ___ . We can pay it easily.
practice.why: afford + able: we can afford it.

practice.q: Nobody was hurt. It was just a moment of ___ .
practice.why: After of, we need a noun: careless + ness.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a tool or an app you use at work or at home. Explain it to someone who has never seen it, in four or five sentences. Use It's a kind of…, Basically… and What I mean is…, and at least two words built with un-, dis-, mis-, -able, -ful or -ness.
yourTurn.model: It's a kind of shared calendar for the whole team. Basically, everyone can see who is free and when. It's really useful, because we used to misread each other's emails about dates. What I mean is, nobody has to ask any more: you just look. The only disadvantage is that it depends on everyone keeping it up to date.

text.title: Customer Support Technician
text.body:
PRACTICE DOCUMENT: this job does not exist

JOB SPECIFICATION
Post: Customer Support Technician (Level 2)
Company: Brightmoor Systems Ltd
Location: Leeds, with hybrid working
Reference: CST-208
Hours: 37.5 a week, Monday to Friday, on shifts between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m.

ABOUT US
Brightmoor Systems supplies online booking software to more than 900 garages, dental practices and hair salons across the UK. Our support team of fourteen handles around 1,200 customer contacts a week.

PURPOSE OF THE ROLE
To provide first-line resolution of client-reported incidents across our cloud-based booking platform, and to escalate unresolved tickets to the second-line team within agreed service levels.

KEY RESPONSIBILITIES
• Triage incoming tickets by priority, and log all customer interactions in the support database.
• Deliver remote troubleshooting to end users by phone, live chat and email.
• Maintain an up-to-date knowledge base of known issues and workarounds.
• Participate in an on-call rota covering one weekend in four.

ESSENTIAL REQUIREMENTS
• A minimum of two years' experience in a customer-facing technical role.
• An IT qualification at Level 3, or equivalent experience.
• Excellent written and verbal communication skills.
• The ability to manage a high-volume workload while meeting response targets.

DESIRABLE
• Familiarity with ticketing software.
• A second European language.

WHAT WE OFFER
• A salary of £28,000 to £31,000, depending on experience.
• 25 days' annual leave, plus bank holidays.
• An on-call payment of £150 for each weekend on call.
• Free parking and a staff canteen.

HOW TO APPLY
Applicants should submit a CV and a covering letter explaining how they meet each essential requirement. Applications that do not address every requirement will not be progressed to interview.
Closing date: 30 October

gist.q: What kind of text is this?
gist.a: a description of a job and the person the company wants
wrong: a contract for a new employee
gist.why: It is a job specification: it lists the duties and the requirements.

gist.q: In simple words, what does this person mainly do?
gist.a: help customers who have problems with the booking system
wrong: sell the booking system to new customers
write new software for the company
gist.why: The purpose is to solve problems that clients report on the booking platform.

detail.q: What happens if the technician cannot solve a problem?
detail.a: They pass it to the second-line team.
detail.why: Unresolved tickets are escalated, which means passed on, to the second-line team.

detail.q: How often does the technician have to be on call at the weekend?
detail.why: The on-call rota covers one weekend in four.

detail.q: An applicant has no IT qualification, but has worked in IT support for five years. Can they apply?
detail.a: Yes, because equivalent experience is accepted.
wrong: No, because the qualification is essential.
Only if they speak a second European language.
detail.why: The requirement is an IT qualification at Level 3, or equivalent experience.

detail.q: What must the covering letter explain?
detail.a: how the applicant meets each essential requirement
wrong: why the applicant wants to live in Leeds
detail.why: Applicants should explain how they meet each essential requirement.

items.meaning: Clear, simple language that anyone can understand, without formal or specialist words.
items.example: The bank has rewritten all its letters in plain English.

items.meaning: Special words used by people in one job or group, which are hard for others to understand.
items.example: The report was full of jargon, so the customers couldn't follow it.

items.meaning: Completely necessary: you must have it.
items.example: A driving licence is essential for this job.

items.meaning: Something that you must have or do, for example to get a job or to pass a course.
items.example: Two years' experience is a requirement for this post.

items.meaning: A person who formally asks for a job, a place on a course or a service.
items.example: We had over sixty applicants for one job.

items.meaning: Equal in value, amount or meaning to something else.
items.example: You need a degree or an equivalent qualification.

items.meaning: Ready to go to work or answer the phone if you are needed, often at night or at the weekend.
items.example: The doctors take turns to be on call at weekends.

items.meaning: How much a person or a team has to do in a certain time.
items.example: My workload doubled when two colleagues left.

items.meaning: A large, organised store of information on a computer, which is easy to search.
items.example: All our customer details are kept in one database.

items.meaning: To write or say something again in a different way, usually to make it clearer or kinder.
items.example: Could you reword this email? It sounds a bit rude.

items.meaning: To make something easier to understand or to do.
items.example: We simplified the form, and now it takes two minutes to fill in.

model.title: The same job in plain English
model.body:
Customer Support Technician, Leeds (some work from home)
£28,000 to £31,000 a year, depending on experience
37.5 hours a week, Monday to Friday, in shifts between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m.

What you will do
You will help customers who have problems with our online booking system. You will answer phone calls, chat messages and emails, and fix as many problems as you can yourself. If you can't fix something, you pass it to a more senior team.
You will record every conversation in our database, and keep our list of common problems and solutions up to date.
One weekend in four, you will be on call. We pay £150 extra for each of those weekends.

What you need
- At least two years' experience of helping customers with technical problems.
- An IT qualification at Level 3, or the same level of experience.
- Clear, friendly English, on the phone and in writing.
- The ability to stay calm and organised when you are very busy.

How to apply
Send your CV and a letter. In the letter, explain how you meet each point under What you need.

write.task: Choose one part of the job specification: Key responsibilities, or Essential requirements. Rewrite it in plain English for a friend who is thinking of applying. Use short sentences and everyday words, and keep every fact. If you prefer, rewrite part of a real job description from your own work.
checklist: I kept every fact, including the numbers.
I replaced jargon, like triage and escalate, with everyday words.
My sentences are short, and each one has one main idea.
A friend outside this line of work could understand it the first time they read it.

card.title: Explain it to a non-expert
card.situation: A friend or a new colleague wants to understand something you know well: a tool, a process or a part of your job. It could also be a hobby, like fixing bikes or baking bread. They know nothing about it.
card.goal: Explain the topic clearly in about two minutes, then answer three or four questions. When an answer is vague, say it again more precisely.

phrases: Let me give you an example.
Does that make sense so far?
prepare.notes: Write your topic in one sentence. Then note one comparison (It's a kind of…), one example, and two questions that a non-expert might ask you.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, explain your topic to a partner who knows nothing about it. Your partner asks at least three questions. Then change roles. Your teacher listens for vague answers and asks you to say them again more precisely.
doIt.wehel: Let's role-play. You know nothing about my topic, and you are curious. I will explain something from my work or my life. Ask me at least four questions, one at a time. If I use jargon or say something vague, ask me what I mean. At the end, tell me which part of my explanation was clearest.

model.title: What does a quantity surveyor do?
lines: Lena
So what do you actually do all day? Your job title means nothing to me!
You
I'm a quantity surveyor. Basically, I look after the money on building projects.
Lena
What, like an accountant?
You
It's a kind of accountant, but for buildings. I work out what a building will cost before anyone starts.
Lena
How can you know that before it's built?
You
Let me give you an example. For a new block of flats, I count everything on the drawings: every brick, every window, every hour of work.
Lena
Every brick? That sounds endless.
You
It would be, but the software does most of the counting. What I mean is, I check the numbers and the prices, and I make sure nothing is missing.
Lena
And what happens if the costs go up halfway through?
You
That depends on the contract. Usually, I agree any changes with the client before the builders carry on.
Lena
So you're the person who says no to expensive ideas?
You
Sometimes! But mostly I help people find a cheaper way to get what they want. Does that make sense?
Lena
Completely. I finally understand your job!
compare: Did you give the general idea first, with Basically or It's a kind of…?
Did you give one clear example?
When an answer was vague, did you say it again with What I mean is…?
Did you check that your listener was following?

canDo: I can explain what a product or a tool does, simply and precisely.
I can work out a new word from its parts.
I can use the right small word after nouns and verbs, like a reason for and depend on.
I can rewrite a text full of jargon in plain English.
I can explain a topic to a non-expert and answer their questions.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Is there a long word you don't know? Split it into parts and guess what it means.
reading.talk: Choose two long words from the text. Split each one into parts and explain what it means. Then say one idea from the text in plain English. Write it, or say it to Wehel.

quiz.q: Sorry, I ___ you. I thought you said Tuesday.
quiz.why: mis- means wrongly: I understood you wrongly.

quiz.q: The new app is very ___ : even my grandfather can use it.
quiz.why: User-friendly means easy for ordinary people to use.

quiz.q: Is this charger ___ with my phone?
quiz.why: Compatible means able to work with another device.
We say a reason for something.

quiz.q: The job advert is full of ___ : words that only IT people understand.
quiz.why: Jargon is special language used by one group of people.

quiz.q: Her ___ is very heavy this month: three projects and a new team.
quiz.why: Your workload is how much you have to do.

quiz.q: The training raised staff ___ of the new safety rules.
quiz.why: -ness turns the adjective aware into a noun.
Work is present simple, so the tag uses do: don't you?

quiz.q: The hotel was lovely. ___ , the breakfast was a bit expensive.
quiz.why: Mind you adds a but and keeps the first point standing.

quiz.q: We met through a ___ friend. We both know Priya.
quiz.why: A mutual friend is someone you both know.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the app conversation in pairs, then explain a different product: a coffee machine, a till, a fitness watch. Then a word-building race: give a root word, and learners build as many words as they can with un-, dis-, mis-, -able, -ful and -ness.

Day 2: the task. Each learner explains a topic from their work or life to a partner who knows nothing about it, then answers at least three questions. Ask learners to repeat any vague answer with What I mean is…
Day 3: talk about the book and answer questions. Then two learners read their plain-English job specifications aloud, and the class checks that no fact is missing.
